'''''Gymnocalycium mihanovichii''''' is a species of [[cactus]] from South America.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Nathaniel L. Britton|author2=John N. Rose|title=The Cactaceae|url=https://archive.org/details/cactaceaedescrip03bri_czc|url-access=registration|accessdate=3 September 2012|date=1 June 1963|publisher=Courier Dover Publications|isbn=978-0-486-21192-3|page=[https://archive.org/details/cactaceaedescrip03bri_czc/page/153 153]}}</ref> 

The most popular cultivars are varied [[mutants]] which completely lack [[chlorophyll]], exposing the [[pink]], [[red]], [[Orange (colour)|orange]], or [[yellow]] [[Biological pigment#Pigments in plants|pigmentation]]; coming from the [[Betalain|betalains]] in the plant becoming exposed.

These mutants, which normally would be unable to survive for even a few days,<ref>NL Britton, JN Rose: The Cactaceae. Descriptions and Illustrations of Plants of the Cactus Family. Volume II. The Carnegie Institution of Washington, Washington 1820, p. 153</ref> are often [[Grafting|grafted]] onto a ''[[Hylocereus]]'' cactus, and the combined plant is called a "moon cactus".<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.succulentsandsunshine.com/faq-items/rescuing-grafting-moon-cactus/|title=Rescuing and Grafting a Moon Cactus {{!}} Succulents and Sunshine|website=www.succulentsandsunshine.com|language=en-US|access-date=2018-11-22}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://baetanical.com/2017/09/10/grafting-101/|title=How to Graft Cacti|date=2017-09-10|work=Baetanical|access-date=2018-11-22|language=en-US|archive-date=2018-11-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181122171938/https://baetanical.com/2017/09/10/grafting-101/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.balconycontainergardening.com/gardening/69-steps-to-grafting-cactus|title=7 Steps to Grafting Cactus|website=www.balconycontainergardening.com|language=en-us|access-date=2018-11-22}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=McCarthy |first=Kat |date=2019-03-19 |title=Controversial, Colorful Moon Cactus {{!}} The Succulent Eclectic |url=https://thesucculenteclectic.com/controversial-colorful-moon-cactus/ |access-date=2026-08-12 |language=en-US}}</ref> ''Hylocereus'' is practically an arbitrary choice, as its only purpose in the graft is to provide nutrients for the mutated plant above it. ''[[Trichocereus]]'' or ''[[Cereus (plant)|Cereus]]'' can also be used.<ref name=":0" />
[[File:Cactus Greenhouses in Mahallat.JPG|none|thumb|233x233px|“Moon cacti” in a [[greenhouse]]]]
“Moon cacti” are commonly grown as [[houseplant]]s.<ref name=":0" /> Unfortunately however, most “moon cacti” do not survive for very long due to drastic differences between the growth rate and size; the ''Gymnocalycium'' usually maxes out at around a few [[Inch|inches]], meanwhile the ''Hylocereus'' grows much larger.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />

==Background==
''Gymnocalycium mihanovichii'' is found growing at lower elevations up to 500 meters in [[Paraguay]] and northeast [[Bolivia]]. The species was discovered there in 1903 by [[Alberto Vojtěch Frič]].<ref>[[Edward F. Anderson]]: The Big Cactus Lexicon . Eugen Ulmer KG, Stuttgart 1905, {{ISBN|3-8001-4573-1}} , p  320 .</ref>

The first description of ''Echinocactus mihanovichii'' was published in 1905 by [[Robert Louis August Maximilian Gürke]]. [[Nathaniel Lord Britton]] and [[Joseph Nelson Rose]] placed it in the genus ''Gymnocalycium'' in 1922.<ref>[[Curt Backeberg]]: The Cactaceae: Handbook of cactus science . 2nd Edition. Volume II. Gustav Fischer publishing house, Stuttgart New York 1883, {{ISBN|3-437-30382-1}} , P.  1881</ref>

''Gymnocalycium mihanovichii'' is very variable, therefore numerous varieties have been described.

==Description==
The individually growing ''Gymnocalycium mihanovichii'' have a broad-spherical, gray-green, often reddish overgrown plant body, which reaches stature heights and diameter of 3 to 5 centimeters. The usually 8 ribs are narrow-edged and slightly notched. The 5 to 6 weak, pliable, and slightly curved [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|thorns]] are greyish-yellow, between 0.8 and 1 centimeter long and partly fall off. The 4 to 5 cm long, bell-shaped to funnel-shaped flowers are yellowish-olive to light olive green. The light green stamens are in two rows. The stylus is also light green; the scar yellowish. The fruits are spindle-shaped.<ref>Urs Eggli, Leonard E. Newton: Etymological Dictionary of Succulent Plant Names. Birkhäuser 2004, {{ISBN|3-540-00489-0}} , p. 154</ref>

==Cultivars==
Cactus can be easily propagated by cutting or offset propagating method.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://succulentsbox.com/blogs/blog/tips-on-succulent-propagation-from-leaves-and-cuttings|title=Tips on Succulent Propagation from Leaves and Cuttings {{!}} Succulents Box|website=www.succulentsbox.com|language=en-US|access-date=2021-11-08}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://succulentsbox.com/blogs/blog/cactus-101|title=Cactus 101 {{!}} Succulents Box|website=www.succulentsbox.com|language=en-US|access-date=2021-11-08}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://succulentsbox.com/blogs/blog/how-to-propagate-cactus-easy-fast|title=How to propagate cactus easy and fast {{!}} Succulents Box|website=www.succulentsbox.com|language=en-US|access-date=2021-11-08}}</ref>

''Gymnocalycium'' produces [[Offset (botany)|offsets]] easily, even when grafted, which can then be [[grafting|grafted]] to a new base, perpetuating the plant. Even the best grafts only last a few years, as the base grows faster than the ''Gymnocalycium''. After that point, the difference in speed between the two becomes too great for the graft to hold together, and so they split apart. The [[scion (grafting)|scion]] can, however, be re-grafted back on to the [[rootstock]] after this.<ref>{{cite book|author=D.G. Hessayon|authorlink = D. G. Hessayon|title=The House Plant Expert|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aNMaWzeffjMC&pg=PA104|accessdate=3 September 2012|date=1 January 1992|publisher=Sterling Publishing Company, Inc.|isbn=978-0-903505-35-2|page=104}}</ref>

The colored species comprise a large group of popular [[mutant]]s, characterized by more or less colored bodies. They can be red, orange, purplish, yellow, or even white. The first totally decolored mutants were called cv. 'Hibotan'. The first only partially de-chlorophyll were called cv. 'Hibotan Nishiki' and can be grown on its own roots. The 'Nishiki' all contain chlorophyll but with many [[anthocyanin]] and appear deep brown. By the time many other colored were obtained and some have special names such as 'Akagurohibotan-Nishiki' or 'Pink-Kuro'.<ref>[http://www.lapshin.org/cultivar/paper/japan-e.htm Cultivar, Japan-E]</ref><ref>[http://www.cactofili.org/specie.asp?mode=&gen=gymnocalycium&sp=mihanovichii+cv%2E+hibotan+nishiki Hibotan Nishiki]</ref>

==Habitat==
A number of ''Gymnocalycium''s prefer [[Shadow|shade]] in the wild, being cloaked under shrubs or grasses, while others prefer abundant [[sunlight]]. Moon cactus, for one, thrives best in bright, indirect light, and can be grown indoors year round. Those preferring plentiful sunshine may need covering from the sun in the hottest months, but exaggerating this will result in loss of flowers. The balance of the [[Container garden|potting]] medium should be adequate to allow decent drainage so that the plants do not sit in marshy soil for more than a day or two after watering. During the summer months, the plant may need frequent watering, though those in small pots would need weekly watering. Nevertheless, the compost should be virtually dry before re-watering. Watering in the winter months is unnecessary. {{Citation needed|date=April 2025}}
